September 2026Turchin Lab, Boston

Extracting bone density results from radiology reports

Bone density reports are written as free text, so using them in research means reading each one. I wrote a rule-based NLP model that pulls the measurements out automatically.

Finding
On 100 reports held out from development, the rules returned 95.0% of the values present, and 99.7% of what they returned was correct.
My role
I built the rule set on the Canary platform, refined it across about 46,000 reports and ran the held-out evaluation. Fritha Morrison and Alexander Turchin supervised.

Jeffrey Bohrer, with Fritha Morrison and Alexander Turchin. Turchin Lab, Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women's Hospital. Presented at Duke's OUSF poster session, September 2026.

Sample DXA report

Made-up text in the formats the rules handle.

Site and sideMeasurementsScanner

This demo is a simplified version written for this page. The real rules run on the Canary NLP platform.

A DXA report has everything a researcher needs, but it's written in sentences, and the wording changes from report to report.

The rules first find the scan site, like the femoral neck or lumbar spine, and which side of the body was scanned.

Then they pick out the bone mineral density, the T-score, the Z-score and the scanner model.

Each site becomes one row in a table. I developed the rules on about 1,200 reports and refined them on about 46,000 more.

On 100 reports the rules had never seen, they found 95% of the values, and 99.7% of the values they returned were correct. For research use, precision matters more here, since a wrong value is worse than a missing one.

Edit the report, or load a less tidy one, to see how the rules respond.

The messy report includes a T-score from an older scan, which the rules skip.
Limitations

All of the reports came from one health system, so the rules may miss formats used elsewhere. They'd need testing on outside reports before being used on new data.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

DXA reports contain the measurements used to diagnose and manage osteoporosis, but they're written as free text, and reviewing them by hand isn't practical for large cohort or longitudinal studies. For a narrow extraction task like this one, a well-tuned rule-based model can do better than machine-learning approaches, and every value it extracts can be traced back to the rule that produced it.

II. Methods

  • Built the model on the Canary NLP platform.
  • Wrote text-replacement rules in Perl and regex to standardize report formats before extraction.
  • Developed the rules on about 1,200 DXA reports, refined them on about 46,000, then on about 400 manually annotated reports.
  • Evaluated once on 100 randomly sampled reports that weren't used in development.

III. Results

At the detection level, precision was 0.997, recall 0.950 and F1 0.973. Precision was at least 0.99 for every variable. The scanner field was the hardest one (recall 0.934, accuracy 0.929).

VariablePrecisionRecallF1Accuracy
BMD1.0000.9460.9720.946
T-score0.9900.9460.9710.943
Z-score0.9900.9600.9780.957
Scanner0.9940.9340.9630.929

IV. Discussion

The model extracted values accurately enough to replace manual review for this task. Because the rules are readable, it's also easy to see why a value was or wasn't extracted, which helps when a new report format shows up.

V. Next steps

The plan is to use the model in clinical research workflows for long-term osteoporosis outcomes research.

May 2026Independent project, Duke

How much energy two AT1R modulators need to enter a membrane

BAM23 and BAM37 bind the angiotensin II type 1 receptor from inside the cell membrane. I used molecular dynamics to compare how hard it is for each one to get there.

Finding
Entering the bilayer costs BAM23 112.1 ± 0.9 kJ/mol and BAM37 29.1 ± 0.3, a difference of 83.0 kJ/mol.
My role
Independent project. I built the simulation systems, ran the steered molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling, and did the analysis.

Jeffrey Bohrer. Independent project, spring 2026, using GROMACS, CHARMM-GUI and Python.

Starting position

Each compound is pulled down on a virtual spring while the simulation measures the force needed.

Steered MD and umbrella sampling in a 128-lipid POPC bilayer at 310 K.

Both compounds start in the water above a POPC lipid bilayer. In steered MD, each one is pulled down on a virtual spring, and the simulation records how much force that takes.

In the water, BAM23 needed about 1.8 times as much force as BAM37 (93.7 vs. 53.4 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻¹).

Both needed more force to get through the charged lipid headgroups.

In the hydrophobic core, BAM23 still needed about 1.5 times as much force.

Umbrella sampling turns this into a free energy cost: 112.1 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for BAM23 and 29.1 ± 0.3 for BAM37, a difference of 83.0. That fits what happened during equilibration, when BAM37 moved into the membrane without being pulled and BAM23 stayed in the water.

Click any layer of the membrane to compare the forces there.

Limitations

The model includes the membrane but not the receptor. The absolute energies are probably too high because of force-field penalties and the fast pulling rate, so the comparison between the two compounds is more reliable than either number alone.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

GPCRs make up about 30% of FDA-approved drug targets. AT1R signals through Gq, which drives vasoconstriction, and through β-arrestin, which has been linked to protective effects in the heart. Our lab identified two biased allosteric modulators of AT1R: BAM23, which favors β-arrestin signaling, and BAM37, which favors G-protein signaling. Both bind sites inside the membrane, so how easily each one enters the membrane could affect how well it works.

II. Methods

  • Built a 128-lipid POPC bilayer in CHARMM-GUI with 5,748 TIP3P waters and 0.15 M KCl.
  • Parameterized both compounds with CGenFF (penalty scores of 71.9 and 66.0).
  • Equilibrated each system with 1 ns of NVT and 1 ns of NPT at 310 K in GROMACS with the CHARMM36 force field.
  • Pulled each compound into the bilayer with steered MD (0.001 nm/ps, 1000 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻² spring, 4 ns) to generate 36 starting configurations.
  • Ran each umbrella sampling window for 5 ns and rebuilt the potential of mean force with WHAM, using 100 bootstrap resamples for uncertainty.
  • Ended the reaction coordinate in the hydrophobic core, since the binding sites are inside the membrane.

III. Results

BAM23 met more resistance than BAM37 in every region of the membrane: −93.7 vs. −53.4 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻¹ in water, −148.1 vs. −120.4 at the headgroups and −151.7 vs. −104.1 in the core. The free energy cost of insertion was 112.1 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for BAM23 and 29.1 ± 0.3 kJ/mol for BAM37, with both maxima deep in the core (z ≈ −0.99 and −0.89 nm). During unrestrained equilibration, BAM37 moved into the bilayer by itself while BAM23 stayed in the water.

IV. Discussion

Both compounds were set up and simulated the same way, so systematic errors should mostly cancel when comparing them. If the difference holds up with the receptor included, membrane access could be worth considering when designing new modulators.

V. Next steps

  • Add the AT1R transmembrane domain to the system.
  • Use QM-refined force field parameters to get better absolute free energies.

December 2025Course research, Duke

Acetylcholine genes in Alzheimer's change differently by cell type

Using spatial transcriptomics data from 72,165 cells in mouse brains, Jorge Mato and I looked at how genes involved in acetylcholine signaling change as Alzheimer's progresses.

Finding
By 13 months, microglia and other glia had upregulated cholinergic genes while excitatory neurons had downregulated them. Normal aging moved the same genes far less.
My role
Joint project with Jorge Mato, covering the gene selection, differential expression testing and spatial mapping.

Jeffrey Bohrer and Jorge Mato. Research report, fall 2025, written in R with Seurat and Quarto.

Cells in a hippocampus section

The layout is a sketch, not real cell positions. The direction of each change comes from our analysis.

Up in AD miceDown in AD miceNo clear change

The dataset (STARmap PLUS) measures gene expression in single cells and records where each cell sits in the tissue.

We grouped cells by type. Neurons carry signals, and glia support them. Microglia are glia that act as the brain's immune cells.

At 8 months, acetylcholine-related genes showed few differences between Alzheimer's model mice and controls.

By 13 months, microglia and other glia had upregulated these genes, and excitatory neurons had downregulated them. Normal aging in the control mice changed much less.

Chrnb2, a nicotinic receptor gene, didn't follow that pattern. It went up in CA3 and inhibitory neurons and down in microglia and the dentate gyrus.

Click a cell type to highlight it and read what we found.

Limitations

This is a mouse model at two time points, so we can't tell which changes come first. The results are associations, not causes.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

Acetylcholine signaling is important for memory, learning and attention, and it breaks down in Alzheimer's disease. Most AD research focuses on amyloid plaques and tau tangles, and less is known about how acetylcholine genes change across cell types over time. Our question was how genes for acetylcholine reception, signaling and breakdown are expressed and spatially organized across cell types as AD progresses.

II. Methods

  • Used STARmap PLUS data covering 72,165 cells and 2,766 genes from AD model and control mice at 8 and 13 months.
  • Identified acetylcholine-related genes with a Gene Ontology search for "acetylcholine", "cholinergic" and "choline".
  • Removed cells with no cholinergic gene expression.
  • Tested differential expression with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction (adjusted p < 0.05, |log₂FC| > 0.25).
  • Separated disease effects from normal aging within each cell type using Δlog₂FC = log₂FCdisease − log₂FCcontrol.
  • Mapped the changes onto 13-month tissue sections and repeated the analysis at the GO-term level.

III. Results

Cholinergic genes on their own didn't separate cell types in PCA or clustering. At 8 months there were few changes (Prkcb, Ly6e and Rgs8 stood out). At 13 months, Apoe, Clu and Bche were upregulated and Nefl and Vdac1 were downregulated in AD mice. Microglia upregulated cholinergic genes and pathways, while excitatory neurons downregulated receptor and signaling genes. In the tissue maps, Psen1 was upregulated widely, Slc44a5 and Crkl stayed downregulated, and the choline transport and acetylcholine response pathways were suppressed across the hippocampus.

IV. Discussion

Neurons seem to lose cholinergic signaling as the disease progresses while microglia become more involved, possibly as an inflammatory or compensatory response. These changes were much larger than the ones from normal aging, so they look disease-driven.

November 2025Knight Lab, San Diego

Non-human microbiome studies share reusable data more often

A lot of microbiome sequencing data can't be reused because the files aren't linked to information about the samples. I built a dataset of 2,147 studies to see which kinds of studies leave usable records.

Finding
Non-human studies had 2.86 times the odds of having a reusable sequencing record, with a 95% credible interval of 1.48 to 5.43. No other predictor separated from the baseline.
My role
I compiled and annotated the 2,147-study dataset and fit the hierarchical model. Samuel Degregori and Rob Knight advised.

Jeffrey Bohrer, with Harrison Gu, Isabella Huang, Harrison Martel, Samuel Degregori and Rob Knight. Knight Lab, UC San Diego. Poster and travel award at ABRCMS 2025.

2,147 microbiome studies

Each square is one study.

Studies from NCBI and ENA. Hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression; lines are 95% credible intervals.

Each square is one of the 2,147 studies I collected from NCBI and ENA and labeled by environment, continent, sequencing type, year and journal.

I counted a study as reusable if it had a Sequence Read Archive accession, then fit a hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression with journal as a random effect.

For most predictors, the 95% credible interval includes 1, so there's no clear difference from the baseline.

Environment was the exception. Non-human studies (animals, soil and other environments) had 2.86 times the odds of having reusable data, with an interval of 1.48 to 5.43. Privacy rules for human samples probably explain part of this.

Publication year showed no trend, so reusability doesn't seem to be improving on its own.

Switch between predictors, or hover over a row to see its estimate.

Limitations

Non-human studies were a small part of the sample, which is why their interval is wide. An SRA accession shows that the data exists, not that it's usable.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

Microbiome studies produce a lot of sequencing data, but much of it isn't linked to metadata about the samples, which makes it hard for other researchers to reuse. Looking at which studies share usable data can point to the practices that cause problems and to publishing standards that could help.

II. Methods

  • Collected 2,147 studies from NCBI and ENA and labeled each by environment, continent, sequencing type, publication year and journal.
  • Counted a study as reusable if it had a Sequence Read Archive (SRA) accession.
  • Fit a hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression with random intercepts for journal, so journals with only a few studies borrow information from the rest (partial pooling).
  • Used weakly informative priors. All R-hat values were about 1.00 and effective sample sizes were above 1,000.

III. Results

Non-human studies had higher odds of being reusable than the baseline (OR 2.86, 95% credible interval 1.48 to 5.43). For the other environments, continents, sequencing types, publication years and almost all journals, the intervals included 1.

I report this as an odds ratio instead of saying non-human studies are "2.86 times as likely" to be reusable, because the two aren't the same when the outcome is common.

IV. Discussion

Privacy restrictions on human data may explain part of the gap. The lack of a trend over time suggests reusability isn't improving without changes to how data gets deposited.

V. Next steps

  • Measure data quality, not just whether an accession exists.
  • Survey researchers about how they share data.
  • Build a web scraper to collect a larger set of studies instead of labeling them by hand.

September 2025Lefkowitz Lab, Duke

Trying to solve AT1R's structure with cryo-EM

Our first attempt didn't produce a usable structure because part of the complex was too flexible. Figuring out why took up most of the project.

Finding
Masking and refining the two halves separately improved the receptor map but not the Fab, which points to flexibility inside the fiducial itself.
My role
I generated the masks, ran the independent refinements and designed AT1R point mutants for the binding-site work, with Samuel Liu and Seungkirl Ahn.

Jeffrey Bohrer, with Samuel Liu, Seungkirl Ahn and Robert Lefkowitz. Lefkowitz Lab, Duke School of Medicine. Presented at Duke's OUSF poster session, September 2025.

One particle

Schematic, not real data.

AT1R is a small membrane receptor, which makes it hard to image with cryo-EM. To make it easier to align, we attached a nanobody, the fusion protein BRIL and a Fab that binds BRIL.

Cryo-EM averages thousands of particle images into one 3D map. If the Fab is rigid, it shows up clearly in the average.

In our 2D classes, both the receptor and the Fab were visible. In 3D, the Fab disappeared. It was moving relative to the receptor, so the alignment followed the receptor and the Fab averaged out.

I masked the receptor and the Fab separately and refined each one on its own. The receptor improved, but the Fab still didn't resolve, which suggests the Fab is also flexible internally.

Drag the slider to change how much the Fab moves. Next, we plan to try CryoROLE to limit that motion, and CryoDRGN or 3D variability analysis to model it.

Limitations

We don't have a final structure yet. What we learned is that this fiducial setup won't work unless its flexibility is dealt with.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

Cryo-EM reconstructs 3D structures from hundreds of thousands of images of frozen particles. GPCRs are small and flexible, and the detergent micelle around them lowers the signal-to-noise ratio, so labs often add fiducials (antibodies, nanobodies or Fabs) to add size and help alignment. That only works if the fiducial is rigid. Our complex had AT1R, the nanobody Nb.AT110i1 to lock the receptor's conformation, a BRIL fusion protein and a Fab that binds BRIL.

II. Methods

  • Smoothed the preliminary map with a Gaussian filter and segmented it into separate masks for the BRIL-Fab and the receptor micelle.
  • Used particle subtraction, defined a fulcrum and ran local refinement on each part in CryoSPARC.
  • Separately, designed AT1R point mutants with SnapGene and BLAST to test where new allosteric modulators bind.

III. Results

Both parts of the complex were visible in 2D classes at 9 Å and 16 Å. In 3D, the alignment favored the receptor micelle and the BRIL-Fab density was lost. Refining the parts independently improved the receptor but not the BRIL-Fab.

IV. Discussion

The BRIL-Fab may be flexible internally, or the masks may need more tuning. Either way, the approach shows how flexible regions can be handled separately during processing.

V. Next steps

  • Use CryoROLE to limit how far the fiducial can move.
  • Use CryoDRGN or 3D variability analysis to model the motion directly.

2025Varghese Lab, Duke

Periosteal injury and long-term fracture pain

Some people have pain long after a broken bone heals. This study tested whether damage to the periosteum, the nerve-rich layer around bone, could be one cause.

Finding
Mice with extensive periosteal injury still showed pain at 12 weeks, along with more nerve fibers at the fracture site and smaller calluses.
My role
I ran the von Frey and dynamic weight-bearing assays and am a co-author. The study was led by Jiaoni Li.

Li J, Shih Y-RV, Tao H, Negus M, Bohrer J, Varghese S. I ran the behavioral pain tests as a research assistant in the Varghese Lab, Duke Orthopaedic Surgery.

Study design

Two groups of mice, followed for 12 weeks after fracture.

Li et al., J Orthop Res 2025;43(6):1155-1163.

All of the mice first got a stabilizing pin.

Four weeks later, each mouse had a fracture. In 10 mice, the periosteum was also injured; the other 9 had the fracture only.

We measured pain for 12 weeks using von Frey filaments, which test sensitivity to touch, and dynamic weight bearing. The mice with periosteal injury still showed pain at week 12.

They also had more nerve fibers at the fracture, more pain-signaling (CGRP+) neurons in the dorsal root ganglia and smaller calluses, which makes this a usable mouse model for long-term fracture pain.

My role

I ran the behavioral assays. The study was led by Jiaoni Li in Shyni Varghese's lab.

Read the full write-up

I. Background

Some patients still have pain years after a fracture, and sometimes it's neuropathic. The periosteum is the most densely innervated part of bone and is often damaged during trauma, but its role in fracture pain wasn't known.

II. Methods

  • Two groups of mice: fracture with extensive periosteal injury (N = 10) and fracture only (N = 9). Fractures were made 4 weeks after pin insertion.
  • Measured pain for 12 weeks with von Frey filaments and dynamic weight bearing.
  • Tracked healing with Faxitron X-ray imaging (callus index).
  • At 12 weeks, used immunofluorescence for CGRP and NF200 in the dorsal root ganglia and flow cytometry for immune cells.

III. Results

Periosteal injury caused severe pain that lasted through week 12. Injured mice had more NF200+ nerve fibers at the fracture site, more CGRP+ neurons and more myeloid immune cells in the dorsal root ganglia, and smaller calluses at every time point.

Li J, Shih Y-RV, Tao H, Negus M, Bohrer J, Varghese S. Extensive periosteal injury during fracture induces long-term pain in mice. J Orthop Res. 2025;43(6):1155-1163.

September 2023The Chronicle, Durham

Science reporting for The Chronicle

In my first semester at Duke, I co-wrote a story about a Duke-led study on an antibody that could help prevent organ transplant rejection.

Finding
An FDA-approved antibody prevented kidney and islet transplant rejection in non-human primates, with fewer side effects than standard immunosuppressants.
My role
I co-reported and co-wrote the story with Vishruth Hanumaihgari.

Vishruth Hanumaihgari and Jeffrey Bohrer. The Chronicle, Duke's independent student newspaper.

The Chronicle, September 20, 2023

Duke-led team finds possible new use for antibody in preventing organ rejection

Immune cells sometimes mark tissues and organs donated from other humans as foreign objects, which prompts an attack.

"It is hard to predict what is going to happen when you give something to humans," Anwar said.

…a sentiment most of the 100,000 people waiting for an organ transplant likely share.

The study, published in Science Translational Medicine, found that an FDA-approved antibody, AT-1501, prevented rejection of kidney and islet transplants in non-human primates.

We had to explain why the immune system attacks donor organs without assuming readers knew any immunology.

We also included the lead author's caution that results can change once a drug is tested in people.

And we connected the study to the more than 100,000 people waiting for an organ transplant.
